## Formal {.unnumbered}

Textbook Source
Book: Introduction to the Theory of Statistics (3rd Edition)
Authors: Alexander M. Mood, Franklin A. Graybill, and Duane C. Boes
Publisher: McGraw-Hill

The Definition
Mood, Graybill, and Boes provide a highly rigorous, set-theoretic approach to defining a statistical population:

"A population is a collection of items (or measurements of items) under study. A population can be finite or infinite. Formally, a population can be considered as a sample space Ω of an experiment. The characteristics of the population are then given by the probability distribution defined over this sample space."
They split this into two rigorous sub-definitions:
- Existent (or Tangible) Population: A concrete, finite set of existing elements, denoted by a finite index set P={1,2,…,N}.
- Hypothetical Population: An infinite set of all possible outcomes that could be generated by a repeatable experiment (e.g., an infinite sequence of coin tosses), which is mathematically represented entirely by its probability law, P(⋅).
